query: For a titanium- and nickel-containing high-entropy alloy in a single-phase solid-solution state, whose elevated-temperature mechanical performance remains unestablished when titanium and nickel serve as primary constituents rather than additions, what single testable intervention hypothesis could produce better mechanical properties under elevated-temperature or extreme-environment testing than the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, mechanism, predicted relative outcome, applicable composition and test-regime boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small, well‐dispersed volume fraction (~0.5 wt.%) of stable nanoscale Y2O3 particles into the feedstock for the titanium–nickel based high‐entropy alloy will refine the grain structure and impede dislocation motion and grain coarsening during high-temperature exposure. This dispersion strengthening intervention is predicted to yield superior elevated-temperature tensile strength and creep resistance compared to the same alloy processed without Y2O3.
generation.material_initial_state: A single‐phase, solid-solution titanium- and nickel-containing high-entropy alloy produced (e.g., by additive manufacturing or powder metallurgy) in a relatively coarse-grained state with a predominantly FCC (or similar) matrix.
generation.intervention: Introduce ~0.5 wt.% nanoscale Y2O3 nanoparticles into the alloy powder prior to consolidation to achieve a uniform nanoparticle dispersion during processing.
generation.conditions: Elevated-temperature mechanical testing in the range of approximately 800–1000 °C under tensile and creep loading conditions, representative of extreme or high-environment applications.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain refinement and the establishment of stable, dispersed oxide particles at grain boundaries and within the matrix, which act as barriers to grain boundary migration and dislocation motion.
generation.mechanism: The Y2O3 nanoparticles are expected to provide a dual strengthening effect: (1) they mechanically pin grain boundaries during thermal exposure, thus reducing grain coarsening and preserving a fine-grained microstructure, and (2) they act as obstacles against dislocation movement (dispersion strengthening), which increases yield strength and retards creep deformation at elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the same alloy processed without Y2O3, the nanoparticle-dispersed alloy will exhibit a measurable increase (on the order of 10–20% or more) in elevated-temperature yield and ultimate tensile strengths, along with extended creep rupture life and improved stability of mechanical properties under extreme environments.
generation.baseline: The identical titanium–nickel based HEA produced without the addition of Y2O3 nanoparticles, subjected to the same processing and testing protocols.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable for single-phase, solid-solution HEAs in which titanium and nickel are major constituents, and the benefits are expected up to temperatures around 1000 °C. It assumes that the Y2O3 addition does not trigger unwanted secondary phase formation or embrittlement over the tested temperature and environmental range.
generation.uncertainty: While evidence from studies on NiCoCr-based superalloys and dispersion-strengthened multi-principal element alloys (e.g., PMC10222657 and PMC7296023) has shown that Y2O3 nanoparticles can significantly refine microstructure and improve high-temperature performance, it remains uncertain how these effects translate to a system where Ti and Ni are primary constituents. Additionally, the compatibility of Y2O3 with a Ti–Ni dominant matrix (as discussed in PMC7040714 and PMC11396108) introduces some uncertainties regarding interfacial reactions or the possibility of deleterious phase formation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of the titanium–nickel high-entropy alloy using an identical fabrication route (e.g., additive manufacturing with identical parameters): one set with a pre-mixed addition of ~0.5 wt.% nanoscale Y2O3 particles and one set without. Both sets should receive the same post-processing heat treatment. Elevated-temperature tensile tests and long-term creep tests should then be conducted in the range of 800–1000 °C under identical loading conditions.
measurements: Tensile yield strength and ultimate tensile strength at elevated temperatures
Creep rupture life and creep strain rates
Grain size and microstructural stability (via SEM/EDS/XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y2O3-dispersed alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (e.g., less than a ~10–20% increase in strength or creep life) compared with the control alloy without Y2O3, or if deleterious phase formation or embrittlement is observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.
